text.intro:
**Two questions.** Should the HIPS correction be applied per site, per season or per filter? And are the season definitions
themselves sound? **Short answers.** Per filter: season explains 15 % of the spread in the correction at
the heavy sites, and a season factor misses the typical filter by 5 %. Seasons are still worth having, as the place
to *check* the correction: at Addis it holds within every season, and what is left is a difference between seasons that is not a loading effect;
at 3 other sites a single season fails.
The calendars hold up: all 42 are complete and consistent, and Addis's is the best split of its climate. A few
are worth a second look, and there is now one measured way to score any of them. FTIR EC is FTIR-derived, HIPS is optical, and no aethalometer
data are used.
text.levels:
**The correction belongs to the filter.** The factor depends on the filter's own optical depth, so the question is
how much is lost by using one factor for a group. At the sites that lose more than a tenth, one factor per site is wrong by 7 %
on the typical filter, one per site and season by 5 %, one per site and month by 5 %.
A season factor still misses by more than a tenth on 27 % of filters. For scale, the ceiling's
own uncertainty is 6 %. **Why seasons do not capture it.** At those sites 44 %
of the spread in the correction is between filters of the same site and season, 41 % between sites and only
15 % between seasons. A season is a mix of light and dark filters, and at Delhi, Jaipur, Dhaka and
Bujumbura of filters sampled at different volumes. **So:** correct each filter. The per-filter factor costs nothing extra, because the optical depth is
already on file for every filter.
text.within:
**Seasons are where to check the correction, not where to apply it.** The check of the procedure page (is linearised HIPS
proportional to FTIR EC?) is run three ways: with all of a site's filters pooled, with each season's own level taken out, and season by
season where a season has 30 filters. **Addis passes within every season.** Bega 1.10 [0.87, 1.39],
Belg 1.04, Kiremt 1.13 [1.00, 1.29]; within seasons
together 1.09 [0.99, 1.21]. Pooled it fails
(0.84). **What is left at Addis is a difference between seasons, not the bend.** After correcting, HIPS per unit of
FTIR EC is 22.3 m²/g in Bega and 16.4 in Kiremt, a ratio of 1.36
(it was 1.69 before, so the per-filter correction removes about half). **At 3 sites a season fails
while the site passes on average:** Johannesburg (winter under, spring over); Kaohsiung (winter under); Beijing (summer under). A pooled check hides these. **Where it stays compressed within seasons** (Delhi, Santiago, Talca),
season is not the explanation: the Chilean sites stay compressed in both seasons, and Talca's filters are too light for loading to be the cause.
Delhi is on the line (0.91 [0.82, 1.00]). **What a season difference
could be:** a real change in how much the aerosol absorbs per unit EC, or FTIR EC reading differently by season. Neither is a HIPS loading
effect, so neither belongs in the HIPS correction.
text.calendars:
**Structure: nothing to fix.** All 42 calendars cover each month exactly once, every site
with HIPS has one, and the Python calendars and the gallery's agree. **New: every calendar scored against the climate.** The calendars are sourced
from agencies and papers, but until now nothing in the repo measured them against weather over a standard period: the gallery's weather covers
each site's sampling period, under a year at CLTA, ETBI, INJA, USSL. This adds 1991–2020 ERA5 normals for
40 sites and asks how much of the year's cycle in rain and temperature falls between a calendar's seasons.
**Addis holds.** Its calendar in use (Bega Oct–Jan, Belg Feb–May, Kiremt Jun–Sep) is the best three-season split there is
(0.88); the older one with February in the dry season scores 0.84, better
on rain and worse on temperature. **Candidates for a second look.** The three Indian sites: the alternative with December in winter fits better at
Kanpur (0.82 against 0.78) and Jaipur
(0.76 against 0.72), and Delhi's older research calendar
(winter Nov–Feb) also scores above the one in use (0.81 against 0.76).
Kaohsiung fits standard quarters better than its shifted ones (0.82 against 0.75);
Taipei the reverse. Bujumbura is the weakest of the sites with HIPS (0.42), and its one-month "short dry season"
is not drier than its rains in ERA5. **What the score is not.** It does not replace a national definition, and ERA5 rain is least reliable in mountains and on coasts. A low
score at a mid-latitude site mostly says rain has no season there.
text.cycle:
**The calendars do carry most of the monthly cycle in filter darkness** where there is one: 75 % at Addis,
73 % at Delhi, 78 % at Pretoria. They carry less at Jaipur
(57 %) and Johannesburg (59 %). **But "wet" and "dry" do not mean
the same thing for HIPS everywhere.** At 11 sites the dark filters come in the dry months (Jaipur, Delhi, Bujumbura, Pretoria, Johannesburg, Mexico City, Bandung, Seoul, Kaohsiung, Abu Dhabi, Beijing). At 5 they come in
the wet months (Santiago, Talca, Addis Ababa, Rehovot, Haifa): at Addis the heaviest filters are in Kiremt, the main rains. So a rule such as "the dry season is the affected
season" would be wrong at Addis. This is one more reason to identify by the filter and use the season only as a label.

[1 rows x 25 columns]. The failure is in one season's aerosol or its FTIR EC, so it should not downgrade the site's other seasons.
After correcting, Bega is 1.36 times Kiremt. That is a season effect in absorption or in FTIR EC, not in HIPS loading.
Structure is sound and Addis's calendar in use is the best three-season split of the climate.
One method for every site, from data now in the repo. It turns 'which calendar' from a choice of citation into something measured.
The alternatives on file fit the climate better at Kanpur, Jaipur and Kaohsiung. Frozen results name their calendar, so a change needs a version, not an edit.
The gallery's ERA5 fields give the rain and temperature of each filter's sampling window. A calendar bin says which months, not what the weather was.
